summary: Critical and sensitive periods represent developmental windows during which neural circuits exhibit heightened plasticity and are irreversibly shaped by experience. This review covers three major domains: visual system development (Hubel & Wiesel's monocular deprivation studies in cats and primates, with critical period ~3 months in cats, ~10-12 weeks in macaques), language acquisition (Lenneberg's critical period hypothesis [age 2 to puberty], Johnson & Newport's 1989 study of 46 Korean/Chinese learners showing discontinuity at puberty, Newport's 'less is more' hypothesis, and Hartshorne et al.'s 2018 mega-study of 669,498 subjects pushing the syntax critical period closure to ~17.4 years), and social/emotional development (Harlow's rhesus monkey studies on contact comfort, Bowlby's attachment theory with critical period of first 2.5 years). Computational models (Achille et al. 2019, Kleinman et al. 2023) demonstrate that critical periods emerge naturally in deep neural networks due to early training dynamics and information-theoretic constraints, suggesting these phenomena may be fundamental to learning systems rather than biological accidents.

key_findings.finding: Hubel & Wiesel (1963) demonstrated that monocular deprivation in kittens during the first 3 months of life causes irreversible loss of visual autognosia responses in the deprived eye, with peak susceptibility at 4-5 weeks where just 1-2 days of deprivation has measurable effects. Adult cat monocular deprivation for 1 year had no effect.

Hubel & Wiesel (1970) mapped the full time course of susceptibility to unilateral eye closure in kittens, showing the critical period lasts from eye opening (~P7) to ~3 months, with maximum vulnerability at 4-5 weeks.

LeVay, Wiesel & Hubel (1980) found in macaques that monocular deprivation at any age from birth to 6 weeks caused equal column shrinkage, with the critical period waning by ~10 weeks and ending by 7 months.
Horton & Hocking (1997) refined the macaque critical period timing, showing eyelid suture at 1 week caused most severe column shrinkage, with susceptibility ending between 10-12 weeks.

Lenneberg (1967) proposed the Critical Period Hypothesis for language, arguing that language acquisition is biologically constrained to the period from approximately age 2 to puberty (~12-13 years), coinciding with cerebral lateralization.

Johnson & Newport (1989) tested 46 native Korean or Chinese speakers who arrived in the US between ages 3-39. They found a strong linear correlation between age of arrival and English grammatical proficiency before puberty (r=-0.87), but no relationship after puberty (r=-0.16), supporting a critical period ending around age 15.

Newport (1990) proposed the 'Less is More' hypothesis, arguing that children's limited cognitive capacities actually facilitate language acquisition by forcing them to analyze smaller, more manageable chunks of input.

Hartshorne, Tenenbaum & Pinker (2018) analyzed 669,498 native and non-native English speakers using a computational model that disentangles age, age of exposure, and years of experience. They estimated that the ability to learn syntax drops sharply at 17.4 years—much later than previously supposed.
A 2021 replication with 1.1 million subjects confirmed that the critical period for syntax closes in late adolescence, validating Hartshorne et al.'s findings with unprecedented statistical power.

Werker & Tees (1984) demonstrated perceptual reorganization in speech perception during the first year of life: infants lose the ability to discriminate non-native phonetic contrasts by 10-12 months while improving on native contrasts. This has been cited over 4,000 times and replicated extensively.

Harlow (1958, 1959) demonstrated in rhesus monkeys that contact comfort from cloth surrogate mothers was more important than feeding for attachment formation. Monkeys isolated for the first 8 months showed permanently impaired capacity for normal affectional responses.

Bowlby (1951) proposed a critical period for attachment formation in the first 2.5 years of life, later extending this to a sensitive period of 5 years. He argued that mothering delayed until after 2.5-3 years was 'almost useless' for most children.
Scott (1962) published 'Critical Periods in Behavioral Development' in Science, synthesizing evidence across species for critical periods in imprinting, social behavior, and sensory development.

Achille, Rovere & Soatto (2019) demonstrated that deep neural networks exhibit critical learning periods: introducing cataract-like visual deficits in early training causes permanent performance loss, while deficits not affecting low-level statistics (e.g., vertical flipping) have no lasting effect. Deeper networks show more pronounced critical periods.

Kleinman, Achille & Soatto (2023) showed that critical learning periods in deep networks govern multisensory integration: networks must be exposed to properly correlated signals during early training or permanently lose the ability to integrate information from diverse sources. Even deep linear networks exhibit this phenomenon.

Tan et al. (2020, 2021) showed in mice that vision is required for the formation of binocular neurons prior to the classical critical period, and that visual experience during the critical period changes the cellular composition of binocular circuitry by recruiting sharply tuned neurons.
